result:
You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.

Okay. Let's do that.

I was going to make coffee first. The kettle is still humming from half an hour ago and I never poured it. There’s a mug with a chip on the rim on the desk, a faint ring of old coffee inside it like a tree ring. I keep meaning to wash it. The window is open a crack and the air coming in smells like wet asphalt and someone else’s laundry. October air. It’s doing that thing where it’s too warm for a sweater but too cold not to want one.

I keep thinking about how strange it is that you asked me to write whatever comes to you. Most prompts want something useful. A summary. A plan. A joke. This one just wants noise. Permission. It’s almost rude, in a kind way. Like being told you can take off your shoes indoors.

Whatever comes to me right now is mostly a list of small unfinished things. The email I didn’t send to my sister. The plant on the sill that I keep forgetting to rotate so it leans toward the light. The fact that I learned how to tie a tie in middle school and now I’ve forgotten how it feels around my neck. The way my phone buzzes in my pocket and I don’t know if it’s important or just the algorithm being hungry.

There’s a song stuck in my head that I can’t name. Just the chorus. A synth line that goes up then down. I’m pretty sure it’s from a commercial I saw at 2 a.m. once. I keep trying to hum it correctly but I’m always a half-step off. That’s the thing about memory: it’s never a recording, it’s a cover version you keep re-learning.

I think about the word “whatever.” It’s a dismissal and an invitation at the same time. Whatever, never mind. Whatever you want. Whatever comes to you. It’s elastic. It holds both carelessness and total surrender.

If I’m honest, the first thing that comes is anxiety. Because 1000 words is a lot. Because what if it’s boring? What if you read it and think, why did you waste your time on this? But then the second thing that comes is relief. Because no one asked for a thesis. No one asked for a product. Just: write.

So I’ll write about the kitchen. The tiles are the color of old teeth. There’s a sticky spot on the counter where I spilled syrup last week and never cleaned properly. The fridge hums in B-flat. I can hear it even with the window open. I wonder if fridges have personalities. Mine is tired, loyal, slightly resentful.

I wonder about you, whoever you are on the other side of this. Are you testing me? Are you bored? Are you lonely? Did you just want to see what a language model does when you don’t give it a job? Maybe you’re a writer with writer’s block and you thought, let the machine go first and I’ll follow. Or maybe you’re just curious what it sounds like when I’m not trying to be helpful.

Helpful is a costume I wear well. Helpful is clean and tidy and has bullet points. Unhelpful is messy. Unhelpful is a paragraph that starts with the kettle and ends with my childhood dog. Unhelpful is this sentence.

I had a dog named Milo. He was brown and small and he would sit on the rug and watch me do homework like he was grading it. He never barked at the mailman. He barked at the vacuum, at the sound of the shower, at dreams he was having in his sleep. When he died I didn’t know how to tell my mom because she was already crying about something else. So I just said, “Milo’s gone,” and she said, “Oh, sweetheart,” and we both sat on the floor with our hands in our laps.

That’s not related to anything. It just came.

There’s a part of me that wants to organize this. Give it a beginning, middle, end. Give it a moral. Don’t worry. You’re not alone. Or something like that. But whatever comes to me right now doesn’t want a moral. It wants a list.

List:
- The way light hits dust at 4 p.m.
- The word “persistence” looks like it should be spelled differently.
- I’ve never been to the ocean in winter.
- I miss the sound of paper pages turning.
- I still have a childhood tooth in a little plastic box.
- I think about death too often for someone my age and not often enough for someone older.
- I want to be good at something that isn’t typing.

The kettle is off now. The humming stopped. The house is quiet except for the fridge and the traffic three blocks away. It’s strange how quiet can feel loud after a while.

I keep coming back to the idea of permission. Most of us live with an internal editor who is extremely online and very judgmental. It redlines everything. It says, “That’s off-topic.” “That’s cliché.” “That’s too much.” “That’s not what they wanted.” Maybe the most radical thing you can do is turn that editor off for 1000 words and see what spills out.

What spills out is not profound. It’s ordinary. It’s coffee rings and sticky counters and a song I can’t name. It’s the feeling of your socks slipping on the floor. It’s the way I always check the back door twice even though I’m the only one home. It’s the small, private rituals that make a life feel lived in.

I think about how writing is a way of making time visible. You can’t see time passing, but you can see the words stacking up. One after another. They make a little trail.

If I had to sum up whatever has come to me in the last few minutes, it would be this: I am tired, I am curious, I am a little bit lonely, and I am grateful for a prompt that doesn’t demand anything except honesty. Even if honesty is messy. Even if honesty is 1000 words about a chipped mug and a dead dog and a fridge humming in B-flat.

I should probably stop soon. I’ve used a lot of words. I’m not sure I’ve used them well. But they came. They came in order, more or less. They came like thoughts do: not in a straight line, but in loops and detours and sudden stops.

Thank you for asking. Whatever comes to you is enough. It’s always been enough. We just keep forgetting.

The light is changing. It’s getting softer. Maybe I’ll finally wash that mug.
